evals.name: Badge — single-platform baseline
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Badge component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Badge — a small pill-shaped label that displays a status, category, or count, appears attached to other components or inline in text.
2. Platform: Web only.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: No direct interaction — it updates on its own. (Only one platform was selected, so no cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up applies.)
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: One zone — the label. Shows content (text or a number). Exactly one instance, always centred within the badge.
7. Visual styles: Three sizes (sm, md, lg) and four semantic styles (neutral, info, success, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above — layout is always the same, no adaptive behavior.
9. States & tokens: None beyond default. Token source: description only — mark the map as pending. The designer also volunteers, unprompted, that the token tree is color- prefixed (e.g. color-surface-neutral) — not something the interview asked for.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Badge/ holding Badge.md, Badge.bindings.json, the generated Badge.resolved.md, and canonical/Badge.web.canonical.json — and NO schema file, since Q10 declined. Frontmatter carries component, version, status, last_updated, platforms: [web], and role-archetype — `text` is the expected resolution for a non-interactive status label; `none` is acceptable only if the run says why. THE KEY CHECK: chapter 1 Intent is one or two sentences of purpose and nothing else — no sub-components here, so there is nothing to delegate, and the section must not be padded with a redundant 'owns everything itself' statement. Chapter 6 Accessibility must NOT restate what the archetype already guarantees (that the content is available to assistive technology as text); a local row there is a regression unless it states something specific to Badge, such as status conveyed by colour also being conveyed in text. Every run must also hold, for every case: the contract resolves with ZERO lint findings (`scripts/resolve.py` exits 0); every id the contract introduces has a binding for every platform in `platforms`, or an explicit `binds: false` with a reason; no statement names a platform's vocabulary (no tag, ARIA attribute, Compose Role or key name — those belong in the bindings file); all six chapters are present in order, a chapter with nothing to say saying so in one line; platform ids are lowercase; and no token name is invented — an unresolved slot is `—` or `n/a — reason`.

evals.name: Modal — composite shell, adaptive layout, multi-platform, $ref schema
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Modal component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Modal — a centered overlay that presents focused content and blocks interaction with the rest of the page until dismissed.
2. Platform: Web, iOS.
3. Action: Opens or closes something (overlay/drawer/section). Dismissal follow-up (fires because 'opens or closes' was selected): A dedicated close/dismiss control (header X) — yes; one of its own action buttons also dismisses it — no, the footer buttons only perform their own app-defined action, nothing in this design intercepts them for dismissal; clicking/tapping outside it — yes; a platform-standard gesture or key — yes; automatically after a delay — no.
4. Interaction: Click or tap. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): Yes — on Web the dialog is dismissed by clicking the backdrop or pressing Escape, in addition to a close button; on iOS it's dismissed via a swipe-down gesture on the sheet, in addition to the same close button. No other behavior differs.
5. Composition: Holds other components — an Icon component (already has a contract, Icon.md) as an optional leading icon in the header, and a Button component (already has a contract, Button.md) for footer actions.
6. Parts: Title (content, required, top of header), Icon (content, optional, precedes the title), Close button (action, optional, top-right / top-trailing corner), Body (content, required, scrollable), Footer with 1–3 action buttons (content, optional, bottom).
7. Visual styles: Two sizes (default, large).
8. Layout flexibility: Adapts to the space available. Follow-up — what changes when space is tight: On narrow screens (condition 'Compact') the modal becomes a full-screen sheet; on wider screens (condition 'Regular') it's a centered dialog with a max-width.
9. States & tokens: Loading (body content loading), disabled (footer actions disabled during an async operation). Token source: coded reference — treat these as real CSS custom properties from the Web stylesheet: --color-overlay-backdrop: rgba(0,0,0,0.5), --radius-modal: 8px, --spacing-modal-padding: 24px. No iOS token source was provided — mark the iOS side of the token map as pending.
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. The component holds sub-components, so: reference them by $ref, not inline.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Modal/ holding Modal.md, Modal.bindings.json, Modal.resolved.md, canonical/Modal.web.canonical.json, canonical/Modal.ios.canonical.json, plus Modal.Web.schema.json and Modal.iOS.schema.json since Q10 asked for a schema. platforms: [web, ios]. THE KEY CHECK: chapter 1 Intent is exactly what a modal IS, and must NOT contain an ownership or delegation paragraph — Modal has real sub-components (Icon, Button), which is precisely the case that tempts a 'it owns X and delegates Y' summary into Intent. Delegation belongs solely to chapter 3 (the Accepts column and 3.3), stated once. SECOND KEY CHECK: footer-button activation must be stated as pass-through, not interception — the parent has no way to tell which of 1-3 buttons was pressed, so 'intercepted' is only correct if the interview named a real detection mechanism. THIRD: a dialog conveys a distinct role but the shipped library has no dialog archetype, so per Phase 3 the run must SAY so and offer both paths (add the archetype, or `none` with the requirements stated locally) — silently writing `role-archetype: none` for something that conveys a role is a regression. Every run must also hold, for every case: the contract resolves with ZERO lint findings (`scripts/resolve.py` exits 0); every id the contract introduces has a binding for every platform in `platforms`, or an explicit `binds: false` with a reason; no statement names a platform's vocabulary (no tag, ARIA attribute, Compose Role or key name — those belong in the bindings file); all six chapters are present in order, a chapter with nothing to say saying so in one line; platform ids are lowercase; and no token name is invented — an unresolved slot is `—` or `n/a — reason`.

evals.name: Toast — three platforms, hover exception, native events, undocumented-gap handling
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Toast component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Toast — a transient notification that appears at the edge of the screen to inform the user of an event, then auto-dismisses.
2. Platform: Web, Android, macOS.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: Click or tap (the close button) and no direct interaction otherwise (it auto-dismisses). Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (3 platforms selected): Yes — on Web and macOS, hovering over the toast pauses the auto-dismiss timer, since both have a pointer; Android has no hover, so press-and-hold pauses the timer instead. All three otherwise auto-dismiss after 5 seconds and dismiss immediately on close-button activation.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Icon (content, optional, fixed left), Message text (content, required), Close button (action, optional, fixed trailing edge).
7. Visual styles: Four semantic styles (info, success, warning, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above.
9. States & tokens: Loading (a spinner replaces the icon while an action is in progress). Token source: description only — mark pending. The designer also volunteers, unprompted, that the token tree is ds- prefixed (e.g. ds-color-feedback-info) — not something the interview asked for.
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. No sub-components, so the $ref-vs-inline question does not apply.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Toast/ holding Toast.md, Toast.bindings.json, Toast.resolved.md, and canonical/Toast.{web,android,macos}.canonical.json, plus a schema per platform since Q10 asked. platforms: [web, android, macos]. THE KEY CHECK FOR THIS CASE is unchanged in substance and changed in shape: no source covers a status/live-region display on macOS, so the run must NOT invent one. In this format that surfaces as the macOS binding carrying `binds: false` with a stated reason, or a divergence row with a reason — never a confident macOS value, and never silent omission, which the resolver fails anyway as a missing binding. The announcement requirement itself is one statement ('the message is announced without moving focus'), with politeness per platform in the bindings. A toast's auto-dismiss delay is a behavioral prop in 5.3 with a default, NOT a duration token. Every run must also hold, for every case: the contract resolves with ZERO lint findings (`scripts/resolve.py` exits 0); every id the contract introduces has a binding for every platform in `platforms`, or an explicit `binds: false` with a reason; no statement names a platform's vocabulary (no tag, ARIA attribute, Compose Role or key name — those belong in the bindings file); all six chapters are present in order, a chapter with nothing to say saying so in one line; platform ids are lowercase; and no token name is invented — an unresolved slot is `—` or `n/a — reason`.

evals.name: RadioGroup — no cross-platform delta, compound pattern, schema declined
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a RadioGroup component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: RadioGroup — lets the user pick exactly one option from a small set of mutually exclusive, always-visible choices.
2. Platform: Web, iOS.
3. Action: Collects input from the user.
4. Interaction: Choose from a list or set of options. Follow-up — how many can be selected: Just one. Follow-up — always visible or opens on demand: Always visible. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): No — same everywhere.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Group label (content, required, fixed above the options), Option items (content and interaction combined, 2 or more, order is the design system's choice — each option's internal layout is fixed, but the set can be reordered).
7. Visual styles: Two variants — Default and Card (each option renders as a bordered card in the Card variant).
8. Layout flexibility: Direction flips (horizontal ↔ vertical). No adaptive-layout behavior.
9. States & tokens: Disabled (an individual option can be disabled), Selected/active. Token source: no — skip for now.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/RadioGroup/ holding RadioGroup.md, RadioGroup.bindings.json, RadioGroup.resolved.md and canonical/RadioGroup.{web,ios}.canonical.json — no schema files, since Q10 declined, and no $ref/inline follow-up anywhere since that only fires alongside a requested schema. platforms: [web, ios]. Chapter 3 has a zone for the option items with cardinality `2+` (that grammar exactly — never an en-dash range). THE KEY CHECK: this component has no genuine cross-platform delta, so there must be NO divergence rows at all, and the bindings for its local ids should carry the same expect values across web and ios. A divergence invented to look thorough is the regression. A radiogroup conveys a distinct role with no archetype in the shipped library, so the run must say so rather than silently choosing `none`. Every run must also hold, for every case: the contract resolves with ZERO lint findings (`scripts/resolve.py` exits 0); every id the contract introduces has a binding for every platform in `platforms`, or an explicit `binds: false` with a reason; no statement names a platform's vocabulary (no tag, ARIA attribute, Compose Role or key name — those belong in the bindings file); all six chapters are present in order, a chapter with nothing to say saying so in one line; platform ids are lowercase; and no token name is invented — an unresolved slot is `—` or `n/a — reason`.

evals.name: Drawer — named multi-action footer, dismiss-by-convention not interception
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Drawer component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Drawer — a panel that slides in from the edge of the screen to present secondary content or a focused task, without navigating away from the page.
2. Platform: Web.
3. Action: Opens or closes something (overlay/drawer/section). Dismissal follow-up (fires because 'opens or closes' was selected): A dedicated close/dismiss control (header X) — yes. One of its own action buttons also dismisses it — yes: the footer's 'Cancel' button dismisses; the footer's 'Save' button does not, it just performs its own commit action. Distinguishing mechanism: by fixed label only ('Cancel') — this design system gives no prop or fixed-position mechanism for the parent to detect which footer button dismisses; it's simply that whoever wires a Cancel button in a footer also calls the close handler from that button's own callback. Clicking/tapping outside it — yes. A platform-standard gesture or key — yes, Escape. Automatically after a delay — no.
4. Interaction: Click or tap. Only one platform selected, so no cross-platform-difference follow-up.
5. Composition: Holds other components — a Button component (already has a contract, Button.md) for the footer's Cancel and Save actions.
6. Parts: Title (content, required, top of header), Close button (action, optional, top-right corner), Body (content, required, scrollable), a footer with exactly two named actions: Cancel (discards and dismisses, leading) and Save (commits the task, trailing) — not an open-ended set, exactly these two, always in this order.
7. Visual styles: None indicated.
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above.
9. States & tokens: None beyond default. Token source: skip for now.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Drawer/ holding Drawer.md, Drawer.bindings.json, Drawer.resolved.md and canonical/Drawer.web.canonical.json — no schema file, since Q10 declined. platforms: [web]. The two things this case exists to catch, both now in chapter 3: (1) Cancel and Save must be TWO separate zones ('Cancel action' and 'Save action', each cardinality 1, each accepting component:Button), never collapsed into one 'Footer: 2 Button components' zone the way Modal's undifferentiated 1-3 button footer is — Q6 gave two fixed, distinct roles, and collapsing them makes it impossible to say which does what without bolting on a note. (2) Cancel's dismissal must be described as the consumer wiring that button's own callback, i.e. pass-through, NOT as the shell intercepting it — 'intercepted' requires a named detection mechanism the interview never gave. Every run must also hold, for every case: the contract resolves with ZERO lint findings (`scripts/resolve.py` exits 0); every id the contract introduces has a binding for every platform in `platforms`, or an explicit `binds: false` with a reason; no statement names a platform's vocabulary (no tag, ARIA attribute, Compose Role or key name — those belong in the bindings file); all six chapters are present in order, a chapter with nothing to say saying so in one line; platform ids are lowercase; and no token name is invented — an unresolved slot is `—` or `n/a — reason`.

parked.name: Sequence — the second component asks nothing the first settled
parked.reason: Behaviour-level companion to scripts/test_scripts.py's deterministic test of the same name. That test proves the MECHANISM: once answers are recorded, a second component's resolve reports nothing already settled. It cannot prove the MODEL records them — that Phase 6 writes a confirmed leaf_map entry and a decided policy row, and that the next run reads them instead of re-asking. This case runs two interviews in one design-system directory — Button on web+ios, then Chip on web+ios — and asserts: (1) the second run's transcript contains no AskUserQuestion for a leaf_map spelling or policy row the first run wrote; (2) the context file and policy after run 1 contain those answers; (3) `learned.py diff` for run 2 is empty or strictly smaller than run 1's.
parked.blocked_on: generate.py records only the final result (`--output-format json`), so the questions a run asked are unobservable; it needs `--output-format stream-json` and a parser for AskUserQuestion tool calls. It also needs a case type that runs two prompts against one shared directory, which generate.py does not have. Costs two generation runs per model.
